unit_label: ABFM Module A unit 2 (courseware unit 2): planning

facts.statement: Planning: the process of engaging in thoughtful discussion before undertaking a task, with in-depth contemplation and attention to detail to be ready with an execution and implementation plan and to save both effort and time; it involves objective analysis of future requirements, deliberate formulation of the design and orderly series of actions anticipated to succeed in accomplishing the goals. Planning covers what is to be done, where, how, when and who will execute. It considers every conceivable risk (losses, defections), and the decisions and directional plans (strategic, tactical or operational) rest on finances, time frame, infrastructure and resources.

Steps in planning (courseware): (1) opportunity analysis: analysing the opportunity and its prospects as the basis for business plans; (2) objective establishment: objectives are the initial step because without them no strategy can be developed; (3) developing planning premises: assumptions derived from forecasting, based on a realistic assessment of the environment, constantly monitored and upgraded, covering forecasting, basic policies and existing plans; (4) alternatives identification: a written record of alternative means, narrowed to the most attractive options; (5) evaluating alternatives: examining strong and weak points, using statistical methods and computers; (6) selecting the best alternative: deciding whether the initial plan or an alternative will be most effective; (7) formulating derivative plans (sub or secondary plans): new policies and procedures, coordination of derivative activities, and working to the targets of the main plan; (8) follow-up and review: planning is continuous, with monitoring and adjustment of the plans as required.

Importance of planning (courseware): helps goal creation (everyone knows the goals, which is the basis of all other management functions); provides direction (efforts are channelled efficiently, guidelines clarify what to do); tackles uncertainty (predictions from existing information help to avoid risk and create another path, with weightage assigned to anticipated functions); discards overlapping and wasteful activities (what, how, why, where and when are addressed in advance, preventing duplication and waste); promotes innovative ideas; facilitates decision making (a guide whenever a manager must take a decision); and controlling (planning and controlling are interdependent: without a concrete objective one cannot see where things went wrong). The courseware adds that a SMART goal is a carefully planned, clear and trackable objective: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Timely.

Advantages of planning (courseware): coordination of various activities; optimisation of resources (activities with maximum demand for resources get optimum allocation for maximum return on investment); inspirations and responsibilities (lessens the likelihood of risk and outlines the commonly anticipated accomplishments); establishment of execution principles (milestones serve as a reference for progress); and adaptability (guiding principles can adjust to change). Basic advantages listed: planning reduces uncertainty, is focused on objectives, facilitates control, encourages creativity and innovation, anticipates problems and copes with change, limits vulnerabilities, works on worker morale, helps accomplish economies, gives managers the upper hand and empowers development.

Disadvantages of planning (courseware): forestalls activity (managers may be so immersed in planning that they have no time to execute, sometimes called "death by plan"); lack of concern (strong systems may lead managers to believe all is well, so they may fail to monitor progress or spot shifts in external circumstances); forestalls adaptability (lower-level supervisors may stick to an arrangement even if it is not working); and hinders innovativeness (people may think they only have to carry out the activities in the plans). Other disadvantages listed: planning takes a significant amount of time; it may rely on untrustworthy data; it can be very expensive; it results in rigidity; it is an exercise in fighting change in a changing environment; it can create a false impression of the organisation's strength; plans may be adapted to the interests of participants; inter-departmental rivalries; human errors; exaggerating the role of possibility; problems of under or over fixation of targets; a false sense of security; a rapidly changing environment; and a manager's daily work schedule may be affected.

Management by Objectives (MBO): the phrase was coined by Peter F. Drucker and first appeared in his book The Practice of Management (1954); MBO is the process of establishing clear parameters for goals, in its most fundamental form a procedure in which management and employees work together to jointly establish, record and monitor goals for a particular period. MBO process (courseware): (1) establish goals and desired outcomes for each subordinate in a conference between the manager and the subordinate; (2) set performance standards; (3) assess performance against goals through frequent performance review meetings; (4) identify reasons for shortfall and give feedback for improvement; (5) establish new goals and strategies for the coming year. Planning is the central idea; employees define measurable personal goals in accordance with the corporate goal. In practice (courseware): establish or alter the goals for the whole company (mission and vision as the base); communicate the goals and priorities (in 1981 George T. Doran used the acronym SMART: specific, measurable, acceptable, realistic and time bound); encourage staff participation in setting individual goals; monitor progress; and evaluate and reward progress. Other steps: organisational goal, employee objectives, monitoring performance and progress, evaluation of performance, feedback and appraisal.

Advantages, limitations and disadvantages of MBO (courseware): limitations: it frequently disregards the culture of the organisation; goals receive greater attention than participation and employee willingness to contribute; managers may emphasise goal setting over operations; it does not place a strong emphasis on the environment (availability of resources, buy-in with leadership and stakeholders); over-dependence on the system can bring problems it is not prepared to deal with. Advantages: a means for determining one's goals and planning to achieve them; it enables a proactive, disciplined approach; it gives the ability to plan for unforeseen circumstances and prepare contingency plans; objectives are measurable so progress can be monitored and altered; more effective use of available resources; an emphasis on the most important aspects of results; improved efficiency, conserving resources and boosting morale. Disadvantages: time-consuming; elaborate written goals and detailed performance appraisals increase paperwork; goals can become out of date and dampen initiative and creativity; too much multi-tasking can cause inefficiency; inability of the subordinate to feel at ease; inflexibility; may make workers' lives more difficult and frustrating; an approach based on rewards and sanctions; and it may lack appreciation by the employees and workers.

Components of a plan (courseware list): objectives or goals; policies or overviews; procedures, directions or rules; programmes or methods; budgets or funding; time schedule; core values, mission or vision; SWOT analysis; and management. Environmental analysis is the process of examining all the factors, internal and external, that affect the performance of the organisation, done systematically and qualitatively; opportunities and threats are the external components and strengths and weaknesses are the internal components. Its steps: identifying, scanning, analysing and forecasting. Advantages: contributes to the accomplishment of goals; identifies and analyses potential dangers; helps understand developments in the commercial environment; creates awareness of impending dangers and opportunities; makes predictions about the future; and helps recognise potential dangers and benefits.

PESTLE analysis (courseware): a method of evaluating the business environment and the potential impact it could have on the performance of the organisation, used to develop business strategies and plans; PESTLE stands for Political, Economic, Social (socio-cultural), Technological, Legal and Environmental factors. The courseware calls them "internal factors" in one sentence, although the factors it describes (government stability, interest rates and inflation, demographics and attitudes, technology, laws and regulations, environmental footprint) are external. Steps: identify the relevance of each factor to the firm; identify and categorise the information for each factor; analyse the data and draw conclusions. Advantages: cost effectiveness, an easy framework, deep understanding, development alertness and opportunity exploitation. Illustrations from banking: political factors (government laws affect banking; the banking sector is susceptible to political influence), economic factors (interest rates, inflation, exchange rates, unemployment, recession affects how much capital banks can access), socio-cultural factors (languages, demographics, attitudes towards consumerism, consumers' desire for a seamless banking experience), technological factors (the Internet changes products, speeds distribution, lowers communication costs), environmental factors (mobile banking reduces paper use and branch visits), and legal factors (privacy, consumer and trade laws, regulatory compliance costs).

Internal environment analysis and tools (courseware): the internal environment is classified by resources and assets: physical resources (plant, machinery, technology); financial resources; distribution network; strategic assets (access to raw material, locational advantage, regulatory protection); network and contacts with outside organisations (suppliers, customers, government, distributors); intangibles (brand equity, goodwill, reputation); and human resources (profile, skill, managerial competencies, organisational structure, culture and values, employee motivation). For a bank this is its branch and IT infrastructure, availability of capital, strengths in a geographical region, brand equity and goodwill and the quality and quantity of its people. Internal analysis reveals strengths and weaknesses. Tools: GAP analysis (to analyse and identify internal weaknesses and performance deficiencies; compares the current position with the projected future position); strategy evaluation (analysing the outcomes of a strategic plan); and SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats; useful because it takes internal and external factors into account simultaneously and gives a comprehensive overview of a company, its products, its brand or a new project at any stage). Strengths are what the organisation does noticeably better than everyone else; weaknesses are areas needing improvement; an opportunity is any factor with the potential to confer competitive advantage; a threat is a potential for harm.

Fixation of objectives, planning premises and evaluating alternatives (courseware): planning begins with the establishment of objectives, a crucial step requiring goals for the organisation as a whole and then for each subordinate work unit; the goals of subordinate departments receive direction from the overarching organisational goals. Planning premises are the planning principles that serve as the basis for the activity of planning: a projection of variables such as the current trend in population, political and economic climate, cost of production, advertising policy, and availability of labour, material and electricity. A forecast is a prediction about the future. The quality of the fixed premises is expected to rest on: the anticipated level of interest in the products, possible production volume, anticipated expenses and the price at which the product might be sold, availability of labour, primary materials and other resources, government economic policy, customers' changing preferences, the impact of emerging technologies and the source of available funds. Criteria for evaluating alternatives: cost, profitability and break-even point; market, sales potential and competitive reaction; ability to meet corporate objectives; strengths and weaknesses; timing; and intuition about success. Finalisation of the plan: an action plan answering the necessary steps, who will undertake the work, how long it will take, where the action will take place and how the work will be completed.

Contingency planning (courseware): contingency plans are alternative plans put into effect if certain key events do not occur as expected; because unforeseen events can make a firm's strategy unsuitable, the contingency plan minimises the risk associated with unforeseen unpredictable events. It is called "Plan B" because it works as an alternative course of action if things do not go as planned. It is more than preparing for catastrophes and natural disasters: it covers the loss of data, staff, clients or commercial relationships. It can be safer or more cost-effective to deal with a risk in other ways (investing in new equipment, sharing the risk by buying an insurance policy) or, for low priorities, to choose not to plan formally. The courseware gives the COVID-19 epidemic as an example of how quickly an entire organisation's way of working may change (everybody working from home). Contingency planning begins by identifying beneficial and unfavourable events that could derail strategies and involves: specifying trigger points; estimating when contingent events are likely to occur; assessing the impact of each event; estimating the potential benefit or harm; developing alternate plans; and making sure the contingency plans are compatible with current strategy and financially feasible. Points to include for each potential risk: landscape, trigger, an overview of the feedback, making people aware of it, important responsibilities and the timeline.

Forecasting (courseware): forecasting is predicting or estimating the future based on evidence from the past and the present; its scope may be comprehensive or limited; it boosts management's confidence but cannot remove the complexity and unpredictability of the future; prediction is the foundation for premises; it uses statistical analysis. Types: long term forecasts (typically three to five years; overarching perspective of the company's monetary requirements and availability of the investable surplus; advantages include improved asset management, systematic leveraging and deleveraging, multiplication of earnings through maintenance of cash reserves and evaluation of variances to monitor performance; disadvantages include the unpredictable nature of the economy, absence of historical knowledge, deficiency of the appropriate range of technologies and limits imposed by silent data); medium term forecasts (for relatively minor strategic decisions; play a crucial role in operational and business budgeting); and short term forecasts (a period of less than one year, typically one to six months; advantages: reduced need for time and money, assessing the current state of the company's finances, performance scenario analysis for preventive action; disadvantages: very high starting price tag due to complexity, payable and receivable accounts are difficult to understand, precision to the granular level is required and late decision owing to limited collaboration). Process: identify and develop the structure (the strategic factors that materially affect the forecast); estimate the future course of business with rational estimates using statistical and other techniques; and analyse deviations in previous forecasts to refine the procedure.

Decision making (courseware): decision making is the actual selection of one course of action from among several alternatives; it is one of the most prominent functions of management and is not confined to planning alone but embraces organising, staffing and controlling; it is a rational process based on systematic analysis of all the relevant facts and not on mere intuition. Hierarchy: top management concentrates on crucial and strategic decisions and broad policies; routine decisions are delegated to middle and lower management. Group decisions: advantages are thorough evaluation of alternatives, easier implementation (a feeling of involvement) and enhanced team spirit; disadvantages are that they are time consuming and costly, disagreements and indecisions (conflicts and blame-games; unanimity is difficult), and no participation or domination (members may shirk responsibility or one dominant member may overshadow others). Conditions: certainty (the decision maker knows exactly what will happen), risk (information is only partly available so probabilities are assigned: objective probability from past experience or subjective probability from intuition) and uncertainty (probabilities cannot be assigned and the likelihood attached to each estimate cannot be measured). Principles: the principle of definition (correct identification of the issues), the principle of evidence (decisions based on evidence are likely to be better) and the principle of identity (consider the viewpoints of all the people involved with an open mind before the final decision).

payload.title: What planning is
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Planning** is **thoughtful discussion and deliberate contemplation before a task**, so that the organisation is ready with an **execution and implementation plan** and saves **effort and time**. It involves an **objective analysis of future requirements** and the **orderly series of actions** expected to achieve the goals.

**Planning covers:** **what** is to be done, **where**, **how**, **when** and **who** will execute.

It weighs **every conceivable risk** (losses, defections). Decisions and **directional plans** (**strategic, tactical, operational**) rest on **finances, time frame, infrastructure and resources**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware describes planning as the foundation for every other function of management.

self_check.prompt_text: What five questions does planning cover?
self_check.expected_takeaway: What is to be done, where, how, when and who will execute.

payload.title: Steps in the planning process
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware lists **eight steps**:

| Step | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 1. **Opportunity analysis** | Understand the **opportunity** and its prospects: the basis for the plans |
| 2. **Objective establishment** | **Objectives first**: no strategy can be built without them |
| 3. **Developing planning premises** | **Forecast-based assumptions** from a **realistic assessment of the environment**; covers **forecasting, basic policies, existing plans**; kept **monitored and upgraded** |
| 4. **Alternatives identification** | A **written record** of alternative means, narrowed to the **most attractive** |
| 5. **Evaluating alternatives** | Examine **strong and weak points**; use **statistical methods and computers** |
| 6. **Selecting the best alternative** | Decide whether the **initial plan or an alternative** is more effective |
| 7. **Formulating derivative plans** | **Sub or secondary plans**: new **policies and procedures**, **coordination**, working to the **main plan's targets** |
| 8. **Follow-up and review** | Planning is **continuous**: monitor and **adjust** the plans |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Derivative plans turn the chosen plan into detailed actions for each unit.

self_check.prompt_text: Which planning step is "selecting the best alternative" preceded by?

payload.title: Why planning is important, and SMART goals
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Importance | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Helps goal creation** | Everyone knows the **goals**; the **basis of all other functions** |
| **Provides direction** | Efforts are **channelled** efficiently; guidelines say **what to do** |
| **Tackles uncertainty** | **Predictions** from existing information help **avoid risk** and create **another path** |
| **Discards overlapping and wasteful activities** | **What, how, why, where and when** are settled in advance, **preventing duplication** |
| **Promotes innovative ideas** | Out-of-the-box thinking to beat competition |
| **Facilitates decision making** | A **guide** whenever a manager must decide |
| **Controlling** | Planning and control are **interdependent**: without a **concrete objective**, one cannot see what **went wrong** |

**SMART goal:** a carefully planned, clear and trackable objective: **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**ealistic, **T**imely.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Measurable and time-bound goals are what make control possible.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the "M" in SMART stand for?

payload.title: Advantages of planning
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Main advantages (courseware):**

1. **Coordination of various activities**: efforts of departments are directed to the goals set in the plan.
2. **Optimisation of resources**: activities with the **maximum demand for resources** get the **optimum allocation** for the **maximum return on investment**.
3. **Inspirations and responsibilities**: staff know the **commonly expected accomplishments** and the **risk is lessened**.
4. **Establishment of execution principles**: **milestones** mark progress and show whether things are **moving as planned**.
5. **Adaptability**: the guiding principles can **adjust to change**.

**Other advantages listed:** **reduces uncertainty**, is **focused on objectives**, **facilitates control**, **encourages creativity and innovation**, **anticipates problems and copes with change**, **limits vulnerabilities**, supports **morale**, helps **economies**, gives managers the **upper hand** and **empowers development**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Milestones turn a long-range plan into checkpoints against which progress can be measured.

self_check.prompt_text: What do milestones in a plan help managers decide?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Whether things are moving as planned and, if not, what adjustments are necessary.

payload.title: Disadvantages of planning
payload.core_explanation_md:
Planning can **harm** an organisation if it is **not carried out as intended**.

| Disadvantage | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Forestalls activity** | Managers may be so absorbed in planning that they **have no time to act** ("**death by plan**") |
| **Lack of concern** | Strong systems may make managers **assume all is well**, so they **fail to monitor progress** or notice **external shifts** |
| **Forestalls adaptability** | Lower-level supervisors may **stick to the plan** even if it is **not working** |
| **Hinders innovativeness** | People think they must **only carry out the plan**, which **stifles creativity** |

**Others:** planning takes **time**, may rest on **unreliable data**, can be **expensive**, causes **rigidity**, can give a **false sense of security**, may be bent to **participants' interests**, and a **fast-changing environment** makes it harder.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The cure for these problems is to review and revise plans continuously instead of treating them as final.

self_check.prompt_text: What is meant by "death by plan"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Planning so much that no time is left to carry out the plans (forestalls activity).

payload.title: Plan components and environmental analysis
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Components of a plan (courseware):** **objectives or goals**; **policies or overviews**; **procedures, directions or rules**; **programmes or methods**; **budgets or funding**; **time schedule**; **core values, mission or vision**; **SWOT analysis**; and **management**.

**Environmental analysis** examines **all internal and external factors** affecting the organisation's performance, systematically and qualitatively. **Opportunities and threats** are **external**; **strengths and weaknesses** are **internal**.

**Steps:** **identifying**, **scanning**, **analysing**, **forecasting**.

**Advantages:** contributes to **goal accomplishment**; identifies **potential dangers**; helps understand **commercial developments**; creates **awareness of impending dangers and opportunities**; makes **predictions**; helps recognise **potential dangers and benefits**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Strategic planners use environmental analysis to predict future trends and set organisational goals.

payload.title: PESTLE analysis
payload.core_explanation_md:
**PESTLE** evaluates the **business environment** and its likely impact on performance, to develop **strategies and plans**.

| Letter | Factor | Banking illustration (courseware) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **P** | **Political** | **Government laws** affect banking; the sector is **open to political influence** |
| **E** | **Economic** | **Interest rates, inflation, exchange rates, unemployment**; a **recession** reduces capital banks can access |
| **S** | **Social (socio-cultural)** | **Languages, demographics, attitudes**; consumers want a **seamless banking experience** |
| **T** | **Technological** | The **Internet** changes products and **speeds distribution** and lowers **communication cost** |
| **L** | **Legal** | **Privacy, consumer and trade laws**; **regulatory compliance costs** |
| **E** | **Environmental** | **Mobile banking** cuts **paper use** and **branch visits** |

**Three steps:** **identify** the relevance of each factor, **collect and categorise** information, **analyse** the data and **draw conclusions**.

**Note:** the courseware once calls the PESTLE factors "internal", but all six are **external** factors; they are taught here as external.

**Advantages:** **cost effective**, **easy framework**, **deep understanding**, **development alertness**, **opportunity exploitation**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: PESTLE looks outward; SWOT combines an outward view (opportunities, threats) with an inward one (strengths, weaknesses).

self_check.prompt_text: What does the first "E" in PESTLE stand for?

payload.title: Internal environment analysis, GAP analysis and SWOT
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Internal environment (by resources and assets):** **physical resources** (plant, machinery, technology); **financial resources**; **distribution network**; **strategic assets** (raw material access, location, regulatory protection); **contacts with outside organisations**; **intangibles** (**brand equity, goodwill, reputation**); **human resources** (profile, skills, competencies, structure, culture, motivation).

**For a bank:** **branch and IT infrastructure**, **capital**, **strength in a region**, **brand and goodwill**, and the **quality and quantity of staff**.

**Tools:**

| Tool | Use |
| --- | --- |
| **GAP analysis** | Identify **internal weaknesses and performance deficiencies** by comparing the **current position** with the **projected future position** |
| **Strategy evaluation** | Analyse the **outcomes** of a strategic plan |
| **SWOT** | **Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats**: considers **internal and external** factors **together** |

**Definitions (courseware):** a **strength** is what you do **noticeably better** than others; a **weakness** is an area **needing improvement**; an **opportunity** is a factor that can give a **competitive advantage**; a **threat** is the **potential for harm** to the organisation.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The point of internal analysis is to see where the organisation excels and where it has gaps, so it can use strengths to counter threats.

payload.title: Objectives, planning premises, evaluating alternatives and finalising the plan
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Fixation of objectives:** planning **begins with objectives**: first for the **organisation as a whole**, then for each **subordinate work unit**; departmental goals take **direction from the overarching goals**.

**Planning premises** are the **assumed conditions** on which planning is based: **population trends**, **political and economic climate**, **cost of production**, **advertising policy**, availability of **labour, material and electricity**. A **forecast** is a prediction about the future. Premises typically rest on expectations about **product demand**, **production volume**, **expenses and price**, **labour and material availability**, **government economic policy**, **customer preferences**, **new technology** and **sources of funds**.

**Criteria for evaluating alternatives:** **cost, profitability, break-even point**; **market, sales potential, competitor reaction**; **ability to meet corporate objectives**; **strengths and weaknesses**; **timing**; **intuition about success**.

**Finalising the plan:** an **action plan** that answers: **what steps**, **who** will do the work, **how long**, **where**, and **how** it will be completed.

payload.title: Forecasting: long, medium and short term
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Forecasting** is **predicting the future from evidence of the past and the present**. It boosts management's **confidence** but cannot remove the **unpredictability** of the future; prediction is the **foundation for premises** and uses **statistical analysis**.

| Type | Period and use | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Long term** | Typically **3 to 5 years**; funding needs and **investable surplus** | **Asset management**, **systematic leveraging and deleveraging**, **cash reserves** build earnings, **variance evaluation** | **Unpredictable economy**, **no historical data**, **limited technology**, **silent data** |
| **Medium term** | **Relatively minor strategic decisions**; basis of **operational and business budgets** | | |
| **Short term** | **Less than one year**, typically **1 to 6 months** | **Less time and money**; shows the **current finances**; **scenario analysis** for preventive action | **High starting cost**, **complex payables and receivables**, need for **granular precision**, **late decisions** |

**Forecasting process:** **identify and develop the structure** (the **strategic factors** that materially affect the forecast); **estimate the future course of business** using **statistical and other techniques**; **analyse deviations in previous forecasts** to improve the procedure.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Reviewing past forecast errors is how a forecasting process gets better over time.

payload.title: Decision making: groups, conditions and principles
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Decision making** is the **selection of one course of action from several alternatives**. It is a **prominent function of management**, **not confined to planning**, and should be a **rational process** based on **systematic analysis of all relevant facts**, not intuition.

**Hierarchy:** **top management** takes **crucial and strategic** decisions and sets **broad policies**; **routine** decisions are **delegated** to middle and lower management.

| **Group decisions** | |
| --- | --- |
| **Advantages** | **Thorough evaluation**; **easier implementation** (a feeling of involvement); **enhanced team spirit** |
| **Disadvantages** | **Time consuming and costly**; **disagreements and indecision** (conflict, blame-games, no unanimity); **no participation or domination** (members shirk responsibility or one member dominates) |

**Conditions of decision making:**

| Condition | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Certainty** | The decision maker **knows exactly what will happen** |
| **Risk** | Information is **partial**, so **probabilities** are assigned: **objective** (from **past experience**) or **subjective** (from **intuition**) |
| **Uncertainty** | **Probabilities cannot be assigned**; the **likelihood cannot be measured** |

**Principles:** **definition** (identify the issues correctly), **evidence** (decide on evidence), **identity** (consider **everyone's viewpoint** with an open mind before the final decision).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Most real managerial decisions are made under risk, with an estimated probability for each outcome.

unresolved: This unit is entirely the courseware's account of general management theory. No regulatory source applies and none was consulted.

The courseware says the PESTLE acronym refers to six "internal factors"; PESTLE factors are external, and the courseware itself calls them external elsewhere in the same section. The items teach PESTLE as external factors.

The courseware describes MBO steps twice with different numbers of steps (a five step process in practice and a five step process in the key concepts); the items teach the process as listed at section 2.6 and 2.6.2 and note the SMART meaning as the courseware gives it in section 2.6.2 ("specific, measurable, acceptable, realistic and time bound") and in section 2.4 (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Timely).

The courseware's description of the MBO process list, the listed advantages and disadvantages and the list of "basic advantages of the planning process" are the courseware's lists; some items on that list are unclear in the courseware ("works with the board by destinations", "works with co-appointment") and are not taught.
The courseware's check-your-progress questions were not used.
